“The 2000 UK IPO market is characterized by the presence of speculative investors, who take part in the IPOs with the intention of reselling them at an even higher price, and the presence of informed investors who have access to information that is unavailable to other investors.
the UK IPO market in 2000 was characterized by a high level of speculation over IPOs.

“the UK IPO market of 2000 was characterized by a high degree of speculation over the new issues which led to an intensification of the two anomalies of underpricing and underperformance, which in turn, can be explained through the behavioural models of Rock and the divergence of opinion.”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the “hot issue” IPO markets on the issuing firms and the investors.
the impact that hot issue markets have on IPOs and their investors and managers.
the effects that the hot issue market has on the IPO market and the performance of IPOs in the long run.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the “hot issue” IPO markets are a consequence of the market participants’ behaviour, which in turn affects the IPOs’ performance.
the 2000 UK IPO market was characterised by a high level of speculation and a high level of short term underpricing.
IPO markets are far from being efficient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IPO market is not a perfect market.

the “hot” IPO markets of 2000 in the UK have had the effect of increasing the level of underpricing, the magnitude of the long run under performance, the level of earnings management and the level of information asymmetry between managers and investors.
, the “hot issue” IPO markets are a result of the market participants’ behaviour and not the cause of it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the “hot issue” IPO markets can be a source of mispricing and that investors should be aware of the implications of this market phenomenon.
the “hot issue” phenomenon is a real phenomenon that has to be taken seriously by investors and regulators.
the IPO market in the “new economy” was driven by the speculative behaviour of investors, which is consistent with the “hot issue” hypothesis.
